newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Juppe promises to go in bid to save poll.
newsitem.headline: France's Juppe promises to go in bid to save poll.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe said on Monday he would resign the premiership whoever won next Sunday's parliamentary election runoff in a last-ditch bid to save his centre-right coalition, outpolled by the left-wing opposition in the first round.
After calling on President Jacques Chirac, Juppe told a meeting of coalition leaders: "We need a new team led by a new prime minister."

The Gaullist premier has borne the brunt of blame for austerity, high taxes and record unemployment in the two years since Chirac took office and was widely held responsible for the conservatives' poor showing in Sunday's first round.
Juppe, 51, is Chirac's longest-serving political associate and aides told reporters only last week that the president hoped to reappoint him if the centre-right won the election.
His decision to sacrifice himself enables Chirac to promise voters a fresh start if they re-elect the coalition rather than forcing him to "cohabit" with a hostile, Socialist-led cabinet.
Socialist and Communist leaders, scenting a possible upset victory, said Juppe's departure was an admission of failure and showed the coalition was panicking.

"This announcement is a sign of the coalition's panic in the face of massive rejection by the electorate. It's just one more incident within the outgoing government and an admission of failure," said former Socialist culture minister Jack Lang.
Communist Party leader Robert Hue said Juppe's departure showed the right was in disarray but he stressed the French people wanted a change of policy and not just a new face.
Political sources said Chirac was expected to address the nation, possibly as early as Tuesday night.
He was unlikely to name a preferred successor to Juppe before the runoff, but he may indicate whether he wants a more socially-minded, or a more free-marketeering policy.

Among prominent candidates are National Assembly president Philippe Seguin, a popular Gaullist Eurosceptic who worries financial markets, and ex-prime minister Edouard Balladur, recently rehabilitated after he fought fellow Gaullist Chirac unsuccessfully for the presidency in 1995.
French stocks plunged on Monday as anxious traders weighed the risk of an upset left-wing victory in next Sunday's runoff, a prospect financial markets had not taken seriously.
The Paris Bourse ended the day 3.91 percent down, but there was no panic on currency markets, which expect a Socialist-led government would go ahead with a single European currency.
The franc traded at around 3.3773 per mark, about a centime lower than last Friday's close.

Final Interior Ministry results showed the combined left polled 40.22 percent, the centre-right RPR-UDF coalition and other moderate rightists 36.50 percent and the extreme-right National Front 14.94 percent. Ecologists scored 6.81 percent.
The left's score adds up to more than 44 percent if the Greens, the biggest ecologist group which has an electoral pact with the Socialists, are counted.

Left-wing parties across Europe rejoiced at their French comrades' gains. German Social Democratic opposition leader Oskar Lafontaine said it showed that "economic and financial policies which raise unemployment through restrictive budgets and social spending cuts are condemned to failure".

Polling institutes projected the left would win a slim overall majority if Sunday's pattern were repeated in the runoff, but they stressed the race was still wide open with the difference in seats between the two blocs equivalent to less than one percentage point of the popular vote.

Much will depend on how National Front supporters vote in the 444 constituencies where their candidate failed to qualify for the runoff, and on whether the right can mobilise some of the 32.09 percent of voters who abstained.

The left pledged vigorous state job-creation measures and a shorter working week without loss of pay to attack record 12.8 percent unemployment. The coalition promised market reforms to scale down state control, cut taxes and free private enterprise.
Ministers dubbed the vote a "warning", a "rebuke" or a "slap in the face" but insisted it did not mean voters really wanted a return to the Socialist-Communist government of the early 1980s.

There was no triumphalism on the left. Socialist leader Lionel Jospin ordered his troops to stay cautious and modest, and Socialist politicians stressed they still had to convince the electorate they were capable of bring about real change.
